transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi. I'm here because my sleep has been messed up for a long time, and no matter how I try to change my schedule, I can't seem to get any real rest. It just feels like I'm constantly running on empty because of it.

When you follow your natural schedule without forcing yourself, do you tend to fall asleep and wake up much later than most people, but sleep normally once you do? Or is it hard to sleep no matter what time you go to bed?

It's definitely hard to sleep no matter what time I go to bed. Even on nights when I'm home and try to sleep on time, I lie there for an hour or more with my mind racing about work quotas and homework. I usually wake up multiple times during the night and never feel truly rested.

When you can sleep in and don’t have to follow any schedule, do you still have trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, or do you sleep normally then? Also, has this been happening for at least 3 nights a week for 3 months or longer?

Yes, even on my days off when I can sleep in, I still struggle to fall asleep and wake up multiple times during the night. This has been happening regularly throughout the week for over two years now, so it's way past the three-month mark.

Do you think your sleep trouble is mainly caused by stress or worry—like your mind racing—or do you also have any medical issues, pain, breathing problems, or substance/medication use that could be keeping you awake?

Yes, it's definitely driven by stress and worry. When I lie in bed, my mind just circles for an hour or more around my work quotas and homework. I don't have any medical issues, pain, or breathing problems, and I don't use any substances or medications that would affect my sleep.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports persistent difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep despite adequate opportunity to sleep, including on days off, with symptoms occurring regularly for over two years. The insomnia is associated with stress and worry at bedtime, and the patient denies medical, respiratory, pain, substance, or medication causes. This is most consistent with nonorganic insomnia.
